title: Gastrointestinal physiology — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Physiology Digestive System lecture + syllabus

questions.stem: The two smooth-muscle layers of the muscularis externa are separated by the
questions.why: Auerbach's (myenteric) plexus lies between the inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle layers and controls motility.

questions.stem: The submucosal (Meissner's) plexus is mainly responsible for controlling
questions.why: Meissner's plexus in the submucosa regulates local secretion, absorption and submucosal muscle.

questions.stem: The submucosal plexus is notably absent from the
questions.why: Submucosal ganglia form plexuses in the small and large intestine but not in the stomach or oesophagus.

questions.stem: The lymphoid tissue that defends the gut against luminal bacteria lies chiefly in the
questions.why: Gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) sits in the lamina propria of the mucosa.

questions.stem: GI smooth muscle behaves as a functional syncytium because its fibres are joined by
questions.why: Numerous gap junctions electrically couple the unitary smooth-muscle fibres, letting them act as a syncytium.

questions.stem: The pacemaker cells that generate the slow waves (basic electrical rhythm) of the gut are the
questions.why: Interstitial cells of Cajal set the slow-wave rhythm that paces GI smooth-muscle contraction.

questions.stem: Slow waves themselves do not cause contraction unless they reach threshold and trigger
questions.why: Slow waves bring the membrane toward threshold; the superimposed spike potentials actually drive contraction.

questions.stem: Noradrenaline and adrenaline affect gut smooth muscle by causing
questions.why: Sympathetic catecholamines hyperpolarise the fibres, inhibiting motility.

questions.stem: A tonic (sustained) contraction, rather than a phasic one, is characteristic of the
questions.why: Tonic contractions maintain closure of the LES, orad stomach, ileocaecal and internal anal sphincters.

questions.stem: The migrating motor complex that sweeps undigested residue along the gut between meals recurs about every
questions.why: The MMC, the inter-digestive 'housekeeper', cycles roughly every 1.5-2 hours and is driven by motilin.

questions.stem: The hormone that initiates the migrating motor complex is
questions.why: Motilin from mucosal endocrine cells elicits the MMC between meals.

questions.stem: Segmentation contractions differ from peristalsis in that they mainly

options.label: B
options.text: mix chyme with secretions rather than propel it

options.label: C
options.text: propel chyme rapidly toward the anus

options.label: E
options.text: are driven by the pharyngeal constrictors

questions.why: Segmentation is a mixing movement that shuffles chyme to and fro; peristalsis is the propulsive movement.

questions.stem: Parasympathetic supply to the distal colon and anorectal region is carried by the
questions.why: The vagus supplies gut down to the proximal colon; the pelvic nerves supply the distal colon and anorectum.

questions.stem: Sympathetic preganglionic fibres to the gut arise from spinal segments
questions.why: Gut sympathetic preganglionic fibres leave the cord between T5 and L2 and relay in the prevertebral ganglia.

questions.stem: In general, sympathetic stimulation of the gastrointestinal tract causes

options.label: A
options.text: increased motility and secretion with sphincter relaxation

options.label: B
options.text: copious watery secretion from all glands

options.label: D
options.text: release of gastrin from G cells

options.label: E
options.text: inhibition of motility and secretion with sphincter contraction

questions.why: Sympathetic activity inhibits gut motility and secretion and contracts sphincters; parasympathetic does the opposite.

questions.stem: Of the roughly 9 litres of fluid passing through the GI tract each day, the amount actually ingested is only about
questions.why: About 2 L is ingested and ~7 L comes from secretions; nearly all is reabsorbed.

questions.stem: Salivary amylase is produced by which type of acinar cell?
questions.why: Serous acinar cells carry zymogen granules containing salivary amylase; mucous cells secrete mucins.

questions.stem: The final saliva reaching the mouth is hypotonic because the duct cells

options.label: A
options.text: are freely permeable to water throughout

options.label: C
options.text: reabsorb more Na+ than the K+ they secrete

options.label: D
options.text: secrete Na+ and reabsorb K+ freely with water

options.label: E
options.text: add large amounts of NaCl to the primary secretion

questions.why: Ducts reabsorb Na+ (more than the K+ secreted) and stay water-impermeable, leaving a hypotonic final saliva.

questions.stem: Unusually among digestive secretions, salivation is controlled

options.label: C
options.text: only by the parasympathetic system, sympathetic having no effect

options.label: D
options.text: purely by neural reflexes, with both ANS branches increasing it

questions.why: Salivary secretion is purely neural, and both parasympathetic and sympathetic stimulation increase it.

questions.stem: Parasympathetic stimulation of the salivary glands evokes saliva that is

options.label: B
options.text: rich in digestive enzymes but low in water

options.label: E
options.text: copious and watery, relatively poor in protein

questions.why: Parasympathetic drive gives abundant watery saliva; sympathetic drive gives sparse, protein-rich saliva.

questions.stem: The parotid gland receives its parasympathetic secretomotor supply from the

options.label: A
options.text: glossopharyngeal nerve via the otic ganglion

options.label: B
options.text: facial nerve via the submandibular ganglion

options.label: C
options.text: vagus nerve via the nodose ganglion

options.label: D
options.text: trigeminal nerve via the ciliary ganglion

questions.why: The parotid is served by IX through the otic ganglion; the submandibular and sublingual glands by VII through the submandibular ganglion.

questions.stem: The pharyngeal phase of swallowing is

options.label: A
options.text: entirely controlled by the enteric nervous system

options.label: B
options.text: involuntary and lasts about one second

options.label: D
options.text: voluntary and under cortical control throughout

options.label: E
options.text: involuntary and lasts about ten seconds

questions.why: Once the bolus reaches the pharynx the involuntary pharyngeal phase takes over for about a second.

questions.stem: During the pharyngeal phase of swallowing, entry of food into the nasopharynx is prevented by

options.label: A
options.text: relaxation of the upper oesophageal sphincter

options.label: B
options.text: elevation of the tongue against the hard palate

options.label: D
options.text: closure of the lower oesophageal sphincter

questions.why: The soft palate rises and seals off the nasopharynx, preventing regurgitation into the nose.

questions.stem: Secondary peristaltic waves in the oesophagus are triggered by

options.label: A
options.text: relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter

options.label: D
options.text: local oesophageal distension via the enteric nervous system

options.label: E
options.text: the swallowing centre at the start of each swallow

questions.why: Primary peristalsis is initiated by the swallowing centre; secondary waves arise from ENS reflexes in response to residual bolus distension.

questions.stem: The swallowing (deglutition) centre is located in the
questions.why: The deglutition centre in the medulla and pons coordinates the swallow via cranial nerves V, IX, X and XII.

questions.stem: Hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor are both secreted by the gastric
questions.why: Parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete both HCl and intrinsic factor.

questions.stem: Pepsinogen and gastric lipase are products of the gastric
questions.why: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen (activated to pepsin by acid) and gastric lipase.

questions.stem: In the parietal cell, H+ is secreted into the lumen in exchange for K+ by the
questions.why: The apical H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) drives H+ into the canaliculus in exchange for K+.

questions.stem: The slight rise in venous blood pH after a meal, caused by bicarbonate leaving the parietal cell, is called the
questions.why: As HCO3- is exchanged for Cl- across the basolateral membrane during acid secretion, blood pH rises transiently — the alkaline tide.

questions.stem: Intrinsic factor is essential because it is required for the absorption of

options.label: D
options.text: vitamin K in the large bowel

options.label: E
options.text: vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum

questions.why: Intrinsic factor binds B12 so it can be taken up by receptor-mediated endocytosis in the lower ileum; its lack causes pernicious anaemia.

questions.stem: Gastrin, which stimulates acid secretion and gastric motility, is released by the

options.label: A
options.text: G cells of the gastric pits

questions.why: Gastrin comes from antral G cells and is triggered by vagal activity, luminal peptides and gastric distension.

questions.stem: During the gastric phase, distension of the stomach wall triggers acid secretion mainly through

options.label: C
options.text: release of secretin from the duodenum

questions.why: Food-induced distension activates stretch receptors driving long vagovagal and short local reflexes that boost secretion.

questions.stem: The intestinal phase ultimately inhibits gastric acid secretion through the

options.label: B
options.text: direct stretch of the gastric fundus

options.label: E
options.text: release of gastrin from antral G cells

questions.why: Once duodenal chyme is acidic and fatty, the enterogastric reflex plus secretin, GIP and CCK inhibit gastric secretion and motility.

questions.stem: Receptive relaxation of the proximal stomach as food arrives is mediated by

options.label: B
options.text: the proton pump of parietal cells

options.label: D
options.text: a vagovagal reflex with NANC transmitters

questions.why: Vagovagal reflexes release NANC transmitters (NO, VIP, ATP) to relax the orad stomach for storage.

questions.stem: The gastric 'pump' that grinds food and controls emptying is the
questions.why: The thick-walled distal stomach produces strong phasic contractions that mix chyme and regulate emptying.

questions.stem: Gastric emptying is characteristically delayed by the presence in the duodenum of
questions.why: Duodenal acid and fat slow gastric emptying so the small intestine is not overwhelmed.

questions.stem: Trypsinogen is converted to active trypsin in the duodenum by
questions.why: Enterokinase from the duodenal mucosa activates trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates the other proenzymes.

questions.stem: Pancreatic proteases are secreted as inactive proenzymes chiefly to

options.label: A
options.text: let them be stored in the gallbladder

options.label: D
options.text: make them soluble in pancreatic juice

options.label: E
options.text: allow them to work at acidic pH

questions.why: Secreting trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen and procarboxypeptidase inactive protects pancreatic tissue from autodigestion.

questions.stem: Secretin, released from duodenal S cells by acidic chyme, mainly stimulates

options.label: E
options.text: enzyme secretion from pancreatic acinar cells

questions.why: Secretin acts on duct cells to secrete a bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralises duodenal acid.

questions.stem: Cholecystokinin, released by duodenal I cells in response to peptides and fatty acids, stimulates

options.label: A
options.text: bicarbonate secretion from duct cells only

options.label: E
options.text: acinar enzyme output and gallbladder contraction

questions.why: CCK drives acinar enzyme output and contracts the gallbladder (relaxing the sphincter of Oddi); it also potentiates secretin.

questions.stem: Most of the pancreatic secretory response to a meal (50-80%) occurs during the
questions.why: The intestinal phase, driven by secretin and CCK, accounts for the bulk (50-80%) of pancreatic secretion.

questions.stem: The liver cells that act as resident macrophages, recycling old red blood cells, are the
questions.why: Kupffer cells in the hepatic sinusoids are macrophages that phagocytose aged red cells.

questions.stem: Hepatocytes receive a dual blood supply of oxygen-rich blood and nutrient-rich blood respectively from the

options.label: A
options.text: central vein and the cystic duct

options.label: B
options.text: splenic artery and the superior mesenteric vein

options.label: C
options.text: hepatic artery and the portal vein

options.label: D
options.text: portal vein and the hepatic artery

options.label: E
options.text: hepatic vein and the bile duct

questions.why: Sinusoids mix oxygenated blood from the hepatic artery with nutrient-laden blood from the portal vein.

questions.stem: The two primary bile acids made by the liver are
questions.why: Cholic and chenodeoxycholic acids are the primary bile acids; conjugation with glycine or taurine forms bile salts.

questions.stem: Bile acids are conjugated with which amino acids to form the more soluble bile salts?
questions.why: Conjugation with glycine and taurine yields bile salts, which act as detergents to emulsify lipids.

questions.stem: While stored in the gallbladder between meals, bile is concentrated roughly

options.label: A
options.text: five-fold by absorbing water and ions

options.label: B
options.text: ten-fold by secretion of bile acids

options.label: E
options.text: not at all, only stored unchanged

questions.why: The gallbladder absorbs water and small ions, concentrating bile about five-fold while retaining organic molecules.

questions.stem: Cholecystokinin promotes bile delivery to the duodenum by

options.label: B
options.text: contracting the gallbladder and relaxing the sphincter of Oddi

options.label: C
options.text: relaxing the gallbladder and contracting the sphincter of Oddi

questions.why: CCK contracts gallbladder smooth muscle and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, releasing bile.

questions.stem: Pre-hepatic (haemolytic) jaundice is characterised by a rise in

options.label: C
options.text: unconjugated bilirubin from excessive red-cell breakdown

questions.why: Haemolysis overwhelms conjugation, raising unconjugated bilirubin; obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin.

questions.stem: Clinically visible jaundice typically appears once serum bilirubin exceeds about
questions.why: Jaundice becomes apparent at a bilirubin of roughly 2.5-3 mg/dL.

questions.stem: Pigment gallstones form in the gallbladder largely because bilirubin, which is not absorbed there, becomes concentrated and precipitates as
questions.why: Unabsorbed bilirubin concentrates up to 10-fold and precipitates with calcium as calcium bilirubinate — pigment stones.

questions.stem: Glucose and galactose are absorbed across the enterocyte brush border by
questions.why: SGLT1 drives Na+-coupled secondary active uptake of glucose and galactose; fructose uses GLUT5, and exit is via GLUT2.

questions.stem: Fructose crosses the brush border membrane by
questions.why: Fructose uses the facilitated transporter GLUT5, independent of sodium.

questions.stem: Salivary amylase contributes little to overall starch digestion because it is

options.label: E
options.text: unable to act on cooked starch

questions.why: Salivary amylase begins starch breakdown but is inactivated by gastric acid; pancreatic amylase completes it in the duodenum.

questions.stem: Lactose is split into glucose and galactose by the brush-border enzyme
questions.why: Lactase, a brush-border oligosaccharidase, hydrolyses lactose to glucose and galactose.

questions.stem: Protein digestion begins in the stomach with pepsin, which works optimally at a pH of about
questions.why: Pepsin, formed from pepsinogen by acid, is most active at pH 1.5-2.5 and is inactivated by the alkaline duodenum.

questions.stem: Di- and tripeptides are absorbed across the brush border faster than free amino acids by a transporter coupled to

options.label: C
options.text: ATP hydrolysis at the apical membrane

questions.why: Small peptides are taken up by an H+-coupled secondary active transporter, then hydrolysed inside the cell.

questions.stem: Dietary lipids are made accessible to water-soluble lipases in the duodenum by
questions.why: Bile acids emulsify fat into tiny droplets, greatly increasing the surface area for lipase action.

questions.stem: Pancreatic lipase requires which cofactor protein to act on emulsified fat droplets?
questions.why: Colipase anchors pancreatic lipase to the oil-droplet surface so it can hydrolyse triglycerides.

questions.stem: After re-esterification in the enterocyte, dietary lipids are packaged as chylomicrons that leave the cell and enter the
questions.why: Chylomicrons are too large for the capillary basement membrane, so they enter the lacteals and travel in lymph.

questions.stem: Lipid digestion products are ferried through the watery layer to the brush border within

options.label: E
options.text: micelles of bile salts and lipid

questions.why: Mixed micelles of bile salts, fatty acids, monoglycerides, cholesterol and phospholipids shuttle lipids to the absorptive surface.

questions.stem: Most water absorption in the gut is driven by

options.label: B
options.text: active pumping of water by aquaporins

options.label: D
options.text: secretion of bile into the duodenum

options.label: E
options.text: a chloride gradient set up by CFTR

questions.why: Water follows osmotically once Na+ and nutrients are actively absorbed; there is no active water pump.

questions.stem: Oral rehydration therapy works because water absorption is enhanced by the coupled uptake of
questions.why: Na+-glucose cotransport (SGLT1) drives sodium and therefore water absorption, the basis of oral rehydration salts.

questions.stem: Calcium is actively absorbed, mainly in the duodenum, by a transcellular route whose entry step and calbindin are dependent on

options.label: A
options.text: parathyroid hormone acting directly on the gut

questions.why: The brush-border calcium channel (TRPV6/CaT1) and calbindin are vitamin D-dependent, so transcellular Ca2+ uptake needs active vitamin D.

questions.stem: Non-haem dietary iron must be reduced from Fe3+ to Fe2+ before uptake, and then crosses the brush border via
questions.why: A brush-border ferrireductase reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+, which DMT-1 carries into the duodenal enterocyte.

questions.stem: Export of iron from the enterocyte into the blood across the basolateral membrane is mediated by
questions.why: Ferroportin 1 exports ferrous iron, which hephaestin then oxidises for binding to plasma transferrin.

questions.stem: The liver-derived hormone that blocks intestinal iron absorption and release from stores is
questions.why: Hepcidin lowers iron availability by inhibiting intestinal absorption and release from stores.

questions.stem: Vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum requires it first to bind
questions.why: B12 binds intrinsic factor (from parietal cells) and is absorbed by receptor-mediated endocytosis in the lower ileum.

questions.stem: The fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) are absorbed

options.label: A
options.text: by simple diffusion in the stomach

options.label: C
options.text: along the pathway for fat, within micelles

options.label: E
options.text: only in the terminal ileum with intrinsic factor

questions.why: Fat-soluble vitamins follow the lipid-absorption route, carried in micelles.

questions.stem: The driving force for fluid secretion by intestinal crypt enterocytes is active movement of

options.label: D
options.text: chloride into the lumen via the CFTR channel

options.label: E
options.text: sodium out of the lumen via the Na+ pump

questions.why: Cl- enters the cell via the basolateral Na+-K+-2Cl- carrier and exits apically through CFTR, drawing Na+ and water into the lumen.

questions.stem: Brunner's glands of the duodenum chiefly secrete
questions.why: Brunner's glands produce mucus that shields the duodenal mucosa from acidic chyme.

questions.stem: The longitudinal muscle of the colon is reduced to three bands called the
questions.why: The teniae coli are three longitudinal muscle bands; their shortening sacculates the colon into haustra.

questions.stem: Strong contractions that sweep colonic contents toward the rectum a few times a day are called
questions.why: Mass movements, unique to the colon, occur three or four times daily, often after meals.

questions.stem: Entry of food into the stomach increases colonic motility and mass movements through the
questions.why: The gastrocolic reflex links gastric filling to increased colonic activity (duodenal distension drives the duodenocolic reflex).

questions.stem: The internal anal sphincter differs from the external one in that it is

options.label: A
options.text: skeletal muscle supplied by the pudendal nerve

options.label: C
options.text: controlled entirely by the sympathetic chain

questions.why: The internal sphincter is smooth muscle (myenteric control); the external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary pudendal control.

questions.stem: The defecation reflex is integrated in the
questions.why: Rectal distension triggers a sacral spinal reflex carried by pelvic parasympathetic nerves, reinforced by voluntary control of the external sphincter.

questions.stem: The chemoreceptor trigger zone that can initiate vomiting lies in the

options.label: A
options.text: area postrema of the fourth ventricle

options.label: E
options.text: dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

questions.why: The CTZ sits in the area postrema at the floor of the fourth ventricle and signals the medullary vomiting centre.

questions.stem: Urea, the main nitrogenous waste, is synthesised by the
questions.why: The liver converts ammonium to urea through the urea cycle; the kidney then excretes it.

questions.stem: Plasma proteins such as albumin, prothrombin and fibrinogen are synthesised chiefly by the
questions.why: The liver synthesises and secretes albumin and the clotting proteins prothrombin and fibrinogen.

questions.stem: The recycling of bile salts from the ileum back to the liver for re-secretion is known as the
questions.why: Bile salts reabsorbed in the terminal ileum return to the liver via the portal vein — the enterohepatic circulation — and are re-secreted.
